newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt bans two weeklies, editors say.
newsitem.headline: Egypt bans two weeklies, editors say.

text.p: Egypt has banned the distribution of two weekly newspapers because of material rejected by the censors, their chief editors said on Wednesday.

Michael Howard, editor at the English-language weekly The Middle East Times, said the censors stopped the distribution of the paper because it failed to remove the front-page teaser to an inside article which it had already withdrawn.
The article, banned by the censors earlier, analysed 15 years of rule by Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.

Ibrahim Issa of the mass-circulation al-Dustour Arabic weekly said the censors banned an edition of his paper without giving him a reason but added he was sure it was because of the paper's staunch anti-Israeli stand.

"They didn't tell us why we were banned but the ban came just 10 days after the Israelis sent (Foreign Minister) Amr Moussa a letter objecting to a picture we ran of (Israeli Prime Min ster Benjamin) Netanyahu with a Nazi swastika on his forehead," Issa told Reuters.
"It intensifies my pain to know that Israel was behind doing this...It's all part of a government campaign of condescension towards its people and their mentality."

An official at the censorship office said that according to a 1936 law, Egypt has the right to control the distribution of publications licensed from abroad. Al-Dustour is licensed in Cyprus and The Middle East Times in Athens.
The censor also did not confirm or deny the ban, referring reporters to the minister of information's office. Officials there were not available for comment.
"By banning an newspaper for four words on the front page, Egypt is somehow shooting itself in the foot," Howard said. The teaser read "Page 3: 15 years of Mubarak".
"We sincerely hope that one day they will realise how futile it is to try and prevent the free flow of information... We're a responsible newspaper and not particularly radical," he added.
The Middle East Times said it was last banned in 1994 because of an article on judicial attitudes to wife beating.
Al-Dustor said it was more recently banned in April and both weeklies have had to remove articles and pictures before Egypt lets them go on sale.

"In 1996 we've had nine articles banned about a wide range of political and social issues and had to run the newspaper with blank spaces. We even had a review about a book on the Middle East banned," Howard said.
In August, the editor of the Cyprus-based Arabic monthly newspaper al-Tadamun said his publication was banned because of an editorial suggesting mental health tests for Arab leaders.
